fields.value: Turn length varied with gaze behavior: more time looking at the speaker was associated with longer turns, with a significant speaker-gaze by gaze-aversion interaction (χ²=374.58, p<2.2e−16); very high gaze aversion shortened turns. Speaker-directed gaze was associated with greater participation unevenness (F(1,137)=4.433, p=.037). For the LC conditions, discomfort varied with gaze measures; warmth had no significant main effects.

fields.value: The paper frames robotic gaze behavior as non-verbal communication that can shape conversational dynamics and human perception. It analyzes speaker gaze, listener gaze, and gaze aversion as robot behaviors.

quotes.text: Consequently, the development of models for robot non-verbal behavior, such as gaze, should be informed by studies of human reaction and perception to that behavior.

We characterize the distribution of robot behaviors taking into account the relative time performing gaze aversion (GA), relative time looking at the speaker (S), and relative time looking at the listener (L).

fields.value: The authors describe gaze as a means of regulating turn-taking and balancing participation; gaze aversion is also described as managing the conversational floor.

quotes.text: Gaze can additionally regu- late conversational dynamics.
Andrist and colleagues [19] showed that robot gaze aversions can be used to manage the conversational floor and improve human perception of robots.
The robot tries to balance participation of the two players through different gaze policies combining the behaviors of looking at the speaker, looking at the listener and averting gaze.

fields.value: More time looking at a speaker was associated with longer turns, more participation imbalance, and higher reported discomfort. The paper notes that gazing a lot at the speaker may work against goals of balancing participation or improving human impressions.

quotes.text: Longer turns by human participants are as- sociated with more time being looked at by the robot while speaking.
Interestingly, interactions where the robot looks more at the speaker appear to be more imbalanced in terms of human participation.
Reported discomfort increases if the participant is looked at more while speaking.
In sum, there is a contrasting trend: more time attending to the speaker leads to longer turns, but more imbalanced participation and discomfort.

fields.value: Furhat used four gaze conditions: a heuristic that looked at the speaker and used gaze aversion; a heuristic that looked at the speaker or listener without gaze aversion; and learned gaze policies using imitation learning or batch reinforcement learning. Gaze behaviors comprised looking at the speaker, looking at the listener, and gaze aversion.

quotes.text: In the Heuristic Condition 1 (HC1, originally control in [9]), the robot only looks at the active speaker and performs gaze aversion.

Heuristic Condition 2 (HC2, originally experimental condition in [9]) tested the ef- fect of a hand-crafted heuristic behavior, where the robot looks at the speaker or the listener, but never performs gaze aversion.

In the Learning Condition 1 (LC1) and Learning Condition 2 (LC2), interaction data from the previous study [9] was used to train a gaze policy for Furhat via imitation learning (LC1, originally IL in [10]) and via batch reinforcement learning (LC2, originally RL in [10]).
The learned gaze policies include three types of behaviors: look at speaker, look at listener, and perform gaze aversion.

fields.value: The paper reanalyzed two studies of two people playing a word guessing game with a Furhat robot that used different gaze policies. Looking at the speaker for more time was associated with longer turns, but also greater participation imbalance and discomfort.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5 — The paper characterizes robotic gaze through speaker gaze, listener gaze, and gaze aversion; examines its roles in turn-taking and participation balancing; reports effects on turn length, participation imbalance, and discomfort; describes heuristic and learned implementations; and names the Furhat robot platform. It does not address embodiment influence (RQ6).
